title: Transit VPC and Private DNS casebook for POC
body:
Summary:
This note collects patterns and pragmatic trade-offs for running a customer POC that needs private networking: multi-account VPC connectivity, split-horizon DNS, secure egress, and private endpoints for Redwood services. Focus is on minimal-risk options for a 2–4 week POC that mirror production patterns without requiring full infrastructure changes in the customer environment.

Goals for the POC:
- Provide a predictable route for traffic from customer app VPCs to Redwood Private control plane and model endpoints
- Keep customer data on private links where possible (no public egress for model payloads)
- Make rollback low-friction and avoid modifying customer global DNS
- Produce an observable baseline: latency, packet loss, DNS resolution times, and end-to-end TLS handshake times

Constraints commonly seen in customer environments:
- Single-account vs multi-account: many customers prefer isolated account per environment; prefer hub-and-spoke patterns
- Limited peering quotas or restricted peering policy with 3rd-party networks
- Corporate DNS managed by a central team with change windows
- Strict egress controls: only allowed via corporate NAT or proxy

Topology options (pros/cons):
1) Direct VPC Peering (customer VPC <-> redwood-private-VPC)
   - Pros: simple, low latency, straightforward route tables
   - Cons: no transitive peering, scales poorly with many VPCs, requires CIDR planning to avoid overlap
   - Typical route table entries: 10.10.0.0/16 -> peering-conn-id

2) Transit VPC / Transit Gateway Hub (recommended for multi-spoke)
   - Pros: supports many spokes, centralizes egress inspection if desired, easier lifecycle in multi-account setups
   - Cons: additional cost, need careful route propagation and propagation filters, potential asymmetric routing if not configured consistently
   - Notes: enable route priority and BGP only when connecting on-prem or partner networks

3) PrivateLink / Interface Endpoints (Redwood as service via AWS PrivateLink)
   - Pros: strongest isolation, no route table changes in customer VPC, integrates with security controls (SGs)
   - Cons: requires service side setup, pricing per ENI, DNS aliasing required for transparent resolution

DNS strategies for POC:
- Option A: Split-horizon DNS on customer resolver (recommended when ops team can add conditional forwarders)
  - Create conditional forwarder for *.redwood.private -> forward to Redwood inbound resolver IPs in hub VPC
  - Pros: no changes to public DNS, low blast radius
  - Cons: requires customer DNS team involvement

- Option B: Private hosted zone linked to customer account (works if customer uses Route53 and allows delegation)
  - Create private hosted zone and associate with customer VPCs; add A/CNAME for service endpoints
  - Pros: simple to manage via IaC; quick to revoke by disassociation
  - Cons: requires AWS account-level permissions and Route53 access

- Option C: Client-side DNS overrides (short-term)
  - Use /etc/hosts or DNSMasq on client nodes for test harness only; low-privilege but not for production

Ingress and endpoint patterns:
- For inbound from Redwood control plane to customer-managed-models: prefer mutual TLS via private endpoints or HTTPs through a customer ALB with security groups restricting Redwood control plane CIDRs
- For customer -> Redwood model endpoints: either PrivateLink endpoints (interface endpoints) or routed via transit gateway to Redwood private subnets

Egress control patterns (how model calls leave customer network):
- Egress via customer-managed NAT/Proxy: simplest for customers that require all egress to be audited and proxied. Ensure proxy supports TLS CONNECT and preserves SNI.
- Forced egress through transit hub with egress inspection (IDS/IPS) when customers require content inspection. Watch for source port translation and ensure sticky sessions not required by model runtime.
- No-public-egress pattern: use PrivateLink for model inference so model payloads do not traverse public internet.

Security controls and least-privilege checklist:
- Security groups: lock interface endpoints to only customer app subnets and Redwood control-plane IPs. Avoid wide 0.0.0.0/0 rules.
- NACLs: keep stateless filters minimal; rely on SGs for stateful control.
- IAM: grant only 'Describe' and 'CreateNetworkInterface' to services creating VPC endpoints; rotate any cross-account roles used for setup.
- TLS: require mutual TLS for control-plane callbacks. Use short-lived certs for POC where possible (Vault or AWS ACM).

Operational notes and gotchas observed in previous POCs:
- CIDR overlap: first failure mode. Always collect customer VPC CIDRs up front and validate against Redwood subnets. If overlap, prefer PrivateLink or transit via on-prem appliance.
- MTU fragmentation when using wireguard/overlay solutions — reduce MTU or enable TCP MSS clamping for tunnels.
- DNS caching at OS level causing stale resolution during failover. Include a flush step in test scripts.
- Asymmetric routing caused by route propagation differences on TGW vs VPC peering. Validate with tcpdump from both sides.

Testing and validation checklist for a 2-week POC:
- Connectivity tests: traceroute, ping (where allowed), curl with --resolve and full TLS handshake validation
- DNS tests: dig for A/CNAME, measure lookup time before/after split-horizon changes - Latency baseline: 50 warm-start model calls and 50 cold-starts (if applicable); capture p95 and p99
- Egress audit: confirm logs at corporate proxy or firewall show expected flows and no unexpected public destinations
- Failure injection: withdraw peering or detach endpoint to test app fallback behavior and rollback plan

Rollback and low-risk deployment recommendations:
- Prefer PrivateLink for POC where customer cannot modify route tables or DNS easily; detach endpoint to rollback
- If using transit gateway, pre-provision route table entries and use propagation toggles instead of deleting resources during rollback
- Keep DNS TTLs low during POC so changes propagate quickly; restore TTLs post-POC

Open questions to capture for each customer POC:
- Who owns DNS change approvals and what is their expected change window?
- Are there IP allowlists on customer side that will block Redwood control-plane IPs?
- Do we need audit logs forwarded to customer SIEM (CloudWatch->Kinesis->Splunk) for compliance?
- Expected QPS and peak tokens/sec to size ENIs/NAT throughput and estimate cost

Appendix: quick command snippets (examples to hand-run during workshop)
- Validate private DNS resolution: dig @<customer-resolver> model.internal.redwood
- Check route table entry: aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters ...
- Test PrivateLink endpoint: curl --interface <eni-ip> https://model.internal.redwood/health -v

Next steps for the Solutions Eng runbook:
- Template an external-facing checklist (for customer ops) with required information (VPC CIDRs, DNS owner, egress path, accept list)
- Create terraform module examples for: transit attachment -> route propagation toggles; private hosted zone -> zone association; interface endpoint consumer module
- Schedule 30-minute DNS pre-check with customer DNS owner before any POC changes

Notes to self: capture network diagrams from customer (png or draw.io) and stash under the POC folder; add latency histograms to the POC dashboard template.
